agents.name: Docetaxel
agents.explanation: Docetaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules. Cells need these to separate their chromosomes during division; disrupting the process can stop cancer cells multiplying. Healthy dividing cells are also affected.

questions.q: When are heart checks due?
questions.a: No routine fixed-cycle echo or ECG is mandated for this regimen alone; assess symptoms and individual cardiac risk. Test timing follows the treatment, clinical findings and local pathway.

questions.q: Where do surgery and radiotherapy fit?
questions.a: Surgery and radiation follow your actual cancer-specific treatment plan. This shared taxane card does not impose an adjuvant breast sequence.

questions.q: Do I need routine CT scans or tumour markers?
questions.a: Agree response imaging and any tumour markers for the actual primary cancer, disease sites and treatment aim. The metastatic breast 2–4-month example is not a universal interval for lung, prostate, gastric, ovarian or bladder cancer.

questions.q: Does a port mean a pump at home?
questions.a: No. This regimen has no routine take-home infusion pump. A port is an access device; the team removes the needle after the visit when appropriate and arranges device removal separately.

questions.q: When do I need blood tests, an ECG or echo?
questions.a: FBC, renal and liver profile before starting and before each 28-day cycle. Check mouth soreness, palms / soles and recovery from earlier toxicity before each dose. ECG is part of baseline and regular monitoring. The NCCP source advises frequent ECG monitoring; the team should specify when it is due rather than assuming an arbitrary cycle interval. Baseline echo / MUGA is required. Repeat during treatment as clinically indicated, and before each additional administration that exceeds a lifetime cumulative anthracycline exposure of 450 mg/m². agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next weekly dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

items.text: The NCCP indication concerns metastatic breast cancer after unsuitable or unsuccessful anthracycline-based treatment. Tumour biology and previous treatments influence options. This page does not describe every early-breast-cancer paclitaxel regimen.

items.text: These are specific later-line settings in this shared protocol. Evidence is less robust than for the breast-cancer weekly comparison. Ask about current alternatives and the implications of use outside the licensed indication where applicable.

items.title: Paclitaxel formulations and combinations
items.text: Conventional paclitaxel and nab-paclitaxel have different formulations and administration requirements. This is a single-agent paclitaxel guide. If another anti-cancer medicine is added, obtain the matching combination guide.

items.title: What matters to you?
items.text: Discuss symptom control, time in hospital, hair loss, neuropathy risk and the activities you most want to preserve. Your priorities can change. Supportive care is available alongside active treatment.

chapters.title: Before each weekly visit
chapters.intro: Use the time between appointments to make review more informative.

items.title: Write down change from your baseline
items.text: Record tingling, numbness, pain, balance, bowel symptoms and fatigue. Tell the team about fever or illness when it occurs; the record is not a reason to wait.

items.title: Check medicines and transport
items.text: Know whether premedication is taken at home or given in hospital. Bring your medicine list and tell the team about a previous infusion reaction. Sedating antihistamines can affect driving.

items.title: Know the agreed schedule
items.text: Check the planned treatment days and blood-test arrangements. A three-visit and four-visit schedule must be distinguished in your own prescription. The number of visits may change after clinical review.

chapters.title: What the checks are for
chapters.intro: Symptoms, blood results and the treatment aim answer different questions.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils protect against infection, haemoglobin carries oxygen and platelets help clotting. A normal previous result or feeling well does not prove the current counts are safe. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate advice.

items.title: Kidney and liver function
items.text: Organ function can change drug exposure. Vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and worsen kidney function. Report reduced urine, poor intake, jaundice and new medicines. The clinical assessment combines results with symptoms.

items.title: Describe symptoms in practical terms
items.text: Tell the team about the worst symptoms since the last visit, even if improved today. Examples include extra stools above your usual pattern, whether mouth pain affects drinking, and whether numbness affects buttons or balance.

items.title: Assessing cancer control
items.text: The review plan may use scans, symptoms and ability to manage daily life. Stable disease can be worthwhile. Ask what benefit would justify continuing and what alternatives would be considered if treatment stops helping.

chapters.title: What to watch for
chapters.intro: Some effects appear early; others build over repeated doses.

items.title: Neuropathy and lasting effects
items.text: Paclitaxel can affect sensation and sometimes strength. Report numbness, burning pain, weakness or difficulty with everyday tasks before the next dose. Symptoms may take time to improve and can persist after treatment.

items.title: Aches and fatigue
items.text: Muscle or joint pain can occur after treatment. Use the agreed analgesia plan and describe how pain affects sleep and function. New extreme weakness, fainting or breathlessness should be assessed rather than attributed automatically to treatment.

items.title: Hair, skin and nails
items.text: Hair loss is common with paclitaxel; it may include body hair. Nail changes and skin symptoms can occur. Ask about practical support and report painful, infected or rapidly worsening changes.

items.title: Mouth, bowels and infection
items.text: Gentle mouth care and early reporting help when soreness affects eating. Report persistent diarrhoea or vomiting. Low blood counts can make infection dangerous; a normal temperature does not make sudden illness safe.

items.title: Infusion and breathing symptoms
items.text: Reactions can occur during infusion despite premedication. Tell the nurse immediately. New cough or breathlessness after leaving also needs assessment; the cause may be infection, a clot, treatment or cancer.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Plan around the activities and people that matter to you.

items.title: Food, drink and practical help
items.text: Use foods and drinks you can manage. Tell the team about weight loss, poor intake or difficulty shopping and cooking; ask for dietitian or practical support. A fixed daily fluid target is not appropriate for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney problems.

items.title: Activity, rest and driving
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Record what fatigue stops you doing. Do not drive when dizzy, unwell or affected by sedating medicines. Ask about work adjustments and transport for treatment days.

items.title: Medicines, vaccines and supplements
items.text: Bring a complete medicine list, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Ask the oncology pharmacist before changes. Discuss vaccination timing. Do not stop prescribed long-term medicines on your own.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment when relevant. Ask for a written contraception and breastfeeding plan covering each medicine and the period after treatment. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy.

items.title: Support for you and your family
items.text: Ask about psycho-oncology, social work, counselling and symptom support. Take information in manageable amounts. A family member or trusted person can help record questions if you wish. Discuss how treatment fits your priorities.

chapters.title: Useful treatment terms
chapters.intro: Short explanations for the clinic conversation.

items.title: Taxane and microtubule
items.text: A taxane is a chemotherapy drug family. Microtubules are small cell structures involved in division and other functions. Effects on these structures help explain both anti-cancer activity and nerve toxicity.

items.title: Premedication and neuropathy
items.text: Premedication is medicine given before an infusion to reduce reactions. Neuropathy means nerve dysfunction. These are separate issues and both need review during weekly therapy.

chapters.title: Benefit, course and continuing checks
chapters.intro: Weekly paclitaxel can shrink or slow metastatic breast cancer. In a breast cancer study it produced more tumour responses than treatment given less often, but more severe nerve symptoms. Some trial participants also received trastuzumab, so the result does not predict every monotherapy outcome.

day_groups.title: Between weekly doses
day_groups.body: Aches, fatigue, nausea or bowel symptoms may occur. Tingling may be mild at first but matters before the next dose. Record what symptoms stop you doing.

day_groups.title: Keep tracking function
day_groups.body: Repeated treatment can increase nerve symptoms and fatigue. Check practical tasks such as buttons, writing and walking. Use the symptom passport to show changes.

day_groups.title: Third weekly review

day_groups.title: After the third visit
day_groups.body: Symptoms may settle or continue. An interval between appointments does not rule out infection or a treatment complication.
day_groups.action: Use the urgent contact plan if unwell and bring your record to the next review.

day_groups.body: A fourth dose is part of the four-visit plan. In the consultant-selected three-visit plan there is no Day 22 infusion. The calendar here is educational.
day_groups.action: Use your confirmed appointment and prescription; call if the schedule is unclear.

day_groups.title: Complete the cycle record
day_groups.body: Record symptoms and functional changes, including those that improve before the next appointment. Treatment continuation depends on benefit, toxicity and your priorities.
day_groups.action: Check the next cycle date and review plan. Do not treat a gap in visits as a guarantee of recovery.

support.title: Premedication for infusion reactions
support.text: Steroid and antihistamine premedication reduce the chance or severity of reactions. The team may adjust premedication after tolerated doses. Do not omit or change it yourself; tell the nurse about missed doses.

support.title: Aches, nausea and bowel support
support.text: Agree a pain-relief and anti-sickness plan. Ask before taking new medicines. Uncontrolled pain or poor intake needs review. Some supportive medicines cause constipation or drowsiness.

support.title: Nerve symptoms and fall prevention
support.text: Use secure footwear and take care with balance, hot surfaces and sharp objects if sensation is reduced. Tell the team early about functional changes; persistent neuropathy may influence dosing.

support.title: Hair, nails and skin
support.text: Ask about hair-loss support and whether scalp cooling is appropriate and available. Protect sensitive nails and skin. Report painful nail changes, spreading rash, blistering or infection.

support.title: Review the full medicine plan
support.text: First-dose NCCP suggested premedication: dexamethasone 8 mg IV, chlorphenamine 10 mg IV and famotidine 20 mg IV 30 minutes before paclitaxel. From Day 8, dexamethasone may be omitted in the source suggested table; add or modify for increased risk or previous reaction under consultant guidance. Famotidine omission is also a consultant/local-policy decision requiring close observation. The conventional paclitaxel product information has a different generic premedication regimen. Reconcile the exact product, weekly NCCP pathway and local policy; never self-omit premedication. Low emetic risk; keep the antiemetic plan separate from reaction premedication. Consider analgesia for myalgia/arthralgia and early action on neuropathy.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Weekly paclitaxel can shrink or slow metastatic breast cancer. evidence.interpretation: The treating team considers the cancer, previous treatment, health and your priorities. Trial averages do not predict an individual outcome.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is specific to the population and schedule studied. Discuss expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own treatment.

questions.q: Which treatment days and breaks should I expect?
questions.a: Eribulin on Days 1 and 8 of each 21-day cycle. Day 15 is a planned treatment-free week. Treatment continues while beneficial and tolerated.

questions.q: When do I need blood tests, an ECG or echo?
questions.a: FBC, renal and liver profile before starting and at the start of each cycle. The EMA product information specifies FBC before every dose, including Day 8; additional renal / liver tests follow clinical need. ECG before starting and during treatment when there is cardiac disease, a slow / abnormal rhythm, QT-prolonging medicines or electrolyte disturbance. Correct low potassium, calcium or magnesium before treatment; repeat monitoring follows risk and findings. No fixed routine echo interval is specified for eribulin alone. Cardiac symptoms or risk prompt individual assessment. If trastuzumab is separately prescribed, use its own cardiac-monitoring plan.

questions.q: When will we know whether treatment is helping?
questions.a: For metastatic breast cancer, ESMO recommends response evaluation generally every 2–4 months, adjusted to disease, treatment and symptoms. For the other cancer indications on this card, use the cancer-specific monitoring plan; the breast interval is not transferred automatically.

questions.q: Where do surgery or radiotherapy fit?
questions.a: These are advanced-disease regimens. Surgery or radiotherapy is used only for a defined local or symptom-control purpose. The oncology and radiation teams decide whether chemotherapy continues, pauses or precedes radiation; no routine overlap is implied.

questions.q: Do tumour markers replace scans?
questions.a: Tumour markers, when useful for the cancer being treated, supplement clinical assessment and imaging. A marker result alone should not determine treatment failure or a treatment change.

questions.q: Does a port mean a pump at home?
questions.a: No. A port is a route into a vein. Staff disconnect the infusion and remove the port needle after the visit when appropriate; removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure.

agents.name: Olaparib (Lynparza)
agents.mechanism: Disrupts DNA repair in susceptible cancer cells
visual: DNA damage accumulates in cancer cells
agents.explanation: BRCA1 and BRCA2 help cells repair breaks in DNA. Some cancers with these changes rely more heavily on other repair routes. Olaparib inhibits PARP activity and traps PARP on DNA, making it harder for those cancer cells to survive DNA damage. Normal blood-forming cells can also be affected, which is why regular blood counts matter.
agents.watch: Keep the four-weekly blood reviews and report persistent nausea, marked fatigue, infections, bleeding or new respiratory symptoms. Severe blood abnormalities need review even if you feel well.

sections.title: After chemotherapy and local treatment
sections.text: Olaparib follows the chemotherapy and local-treatment plan. In OlympiA, surgery and any indicated radiotherapy were completed before olaparib, with at least a two-week gap after local treatment. NCCP advises starting ideally within twelve weeks of the last surgery, chemotherapy or radiation; your team sets the start.

sections.title: Endocrine therapy may overlap
sections.text: For hormone receptor-positive disease, the prescribed hormone treatment can continue alongside olaparib and often continues after the one-year olaparib course. Its injections, tablets and bone checks keep their own schedule.

sections.title: A daily routine at home
sections.text: Choose consistent morning and evening times and check the strength and number of tablets on each new prescription. Keep a sufficient supply before weekends or holidays. No infusion pump or port is needed for olaparib itself.

sections.title: If treatment is paused
sections.text: The oncology team decides when and at what dose to restart after blood recovery or symptom improvement. Do not calculate a catch-up dose or restart automatically because a calendar month has passed.

sections.title: After the planned year
sections.text: Agree the stop date and ongoing breast follow-up. Endocrine treatment and breast surveillance may continue. Report persistent unexplained fatigue, infections, bruising or breathlessness even after olaparib finishes.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: In people with the high-risk inherited BRCA-associated breast cancer studied, one year of olaparib reduced invasive recurrence and improved survival. Longer follow-up shows that the benefit persists after treatment ends. Eligibility is specific, and benefit for an individual remains uncertain.
evidence.population: NCCP 00588 h only: germline pathogenic BRCA1/2-associated HER2-negative high-risk early breast cancer after neoadjuvant/adjuvant chemotherapy. Do not route other 00588 indications into this breast suite.
evidence.interpretation: The treating team considers the cancer, previous treatment, health and your priorities. Trial averages do not predict an individual outcome.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is specific to the population and schedule studied. Discuss expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own treatment.

chapters.title: The exact treatment being discussed
chapters.intro: Reduce the chance of invasive recurrence after standard chemotherapy and local treatment. It may be taken alongside prescribed endocrine therapy for hormone receptor-positive disease.

items.title: Who this covers
items.text: Adults with a confirmed pathogenic germline BRCA1/2 mutation, HER2-negative high-risk early breast cancer and previous neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy. The high-risk definition depends on hormone receptors, prior chemotherapy setting, surgical pathology and, for one pathway, CPS+EG score.

items.title: Dose and administration
items.text: Usually 300 mg twice daily; follow the individual prescription. Swallow tablets whole with water, with or without food. Do not chew, crush, dissolve or divide them. If a dose is missed, take the next normal dose at its usual time; do not double it. Check tablet strength after any dose change.

items.title: Duration and decisions
items.text: For breast indication 00588 h: up to one year, or earlier if the cancer recurs or side effects make treatment unsuitable. This is different from olaparib durations in ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Individual safety and source differences

chapters.title: Checks throughout treatment
chapters.intro: Blood tests assess treatment safety. Scans assess disease or investigate symptoms. Echo and ECG answer different questions.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Confirm the germline BRCA result and breast eligibility. Review blood count, kidney and liver tests, recovery from previous treatment, medicines and supplements, and pregnancy testing where relevant. Confirm the surgery/radiotherapy sequence and the planned start.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: NCCP specifies FBC, kidney and liver tests every four weeks for the first twelve months. Reviews also assess nausea, appetite, energy, bruising, infections and breathing symptoms. Extra tests or an interruption may be needed if results or symptoms change.

items.title: Heart checks
items.text: Olaparib alone has no routine ECG or echo surveillance timetable in this NCCP regimen. Heart checks may still be needed because of previous anthracycline/HER2 treatment, existing disease or new symptoms.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: There is no olaparib-specific DXA schedule. If an aromatase inhibitor or ovarian suppression is also prescribed, retain that treatment’s separate bone-density and bone-health plan.

chapters.title: Your wider treatment plan
chapters.intro: Additional treatments depend on the confirmed setting and indication.

items.title: Early-breast follow-up
items.text: After early breast cancer treatment, annual mammography is generally used for remaining breast tissue: both breasts after conservation, or the opposite breast after unilateral mastectomy. Routine mammography of the mastectomy side is not required. Routine CT, bone scans and tumour markers are not recommended solely to look for recurrence in an asymptomatic person. Safety blood tests for ongoing olaparib are a separate requirement. New symptoms need assessment between appointments.

items.title: Tumour markers
items.text: No routine tumour-marker surveillance for asymptomatic early breast cancer.

items.title: Pregnancy, fertility and contraception
items.text: Olaparib can harm an unborn baby. Discuss effective contraception before treatment; EMA recommends two reliable complementary methods for women during treatment and for six months afterwards. Men and their partners need contraception during treatment and for three months afterwards. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for one month after the last dose.

chapters.title: Evidence depends on the population
chapters.intro: Different studies answer different questions; do not compare their results as if populations and follow-up were identical.

items.title: OlympiA: four-year survival analysis
items.text: The earlier survival update showed that the benefit extended beyond preventing invasive recurrence. These results apply to the selected high-risk inherited BRCA-associated early breast population, not every HER2-negative breast cancer.

items.title: OlympiA: sustained benefit at six years
items.text: Longer follow-up confirms that reductions in invasive recurrence and improvements in survival persist after the planned year of treatment. This is follow-up after one year of olaparib, not a longer prescribed course; rare late marrow effects still need attention.

Aprepitant is a moderate CYP3A inhibitor in NCCP 00588 and can increase olaparib exposure. The prescriber/pharmacist should choose and reconcile supportive medicines; never add an antiemetic from another regimen without checking.
Anaemia or other low counts can lead to interruption, dose adjustment, transfusion or additional investigation. There is no universal routine G-CSF course for every person on this regimen.

Review all prescriptions, over-the-counter drugs and herbal products. Strong/moderate CYP3A inhibitors or inducers can change exposure. Avoid grapefruit products and seek advice before starting anything new.
NCCP allows consideration of a proton pump inhibitor under local policy. This is symptom- and patient-dependent, rather than a compulsory medication for everyone.

Agree an oral antiemetic prevention / rescue plan before treatment. Continuous oral treatment does not use the Day 1–4 IV chemotherapy template. Confirm agent, dose, frequency, duration and interactions; no default daily steroid order.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.
